paragraphs.text: For seven days our ship had been tossed at sea. The broken masts had gone overboard. Leaks had sprung everywhere, and the water was rising rapidly as the raging storm grew stronger.

My wife, Elizabeth, gathered our four young sons around her in our cabin. She was encouraging them with calm and loving words. This was not the scene we had pictured when we set out from Switzerland to establish a new colony.
Amid the roar of the thundering waves, I suddenly heard a seaman cry, "Land! Land!"
At the same instant, the ship struck something with a jolt that threw everyone to the deck of the cabin.
Above the dreadful sounds of the ship breaking up, I heard the captain shout, "Lower the lifeboats! Abandon ship!"
"Abandon ship!" I exclaimed. The words went like a dagger through my heart. But seeing my children's terror, I hid my own fear.
"Take courage, my boys!" I cried. "We're all still above water. There is land nearby. Let's do our best to reach it."

With that I went up on deck. Imagine my horror when I saw all the lifeboats out on the water. The crew had abandoned us! But as I looked around in despair, I realized that our situation was not hopeless. Although the bow of the ship had been destroyed, our cabin remained unbroken in the stern. I could just make out some land through the rain.
I returned to my family and forced a smile. "If the wind and waves die down tomorrow, we can go ashore."
"Then we must find food," said my wife. "We'll need all our strength tomorrow."
After a good supper, the three youngest boys—Ernest, 13; Jack, 11; and Franz, 8—were soon asleep. But at 15, Fritz was old enough to understand the danger and to stay up with us.
"Father, you and I can swim," he said. "But don't you think we should make life preservers for Mother and the boys?"
"An excellent idea!" I told Fritz. "Let's make some right now in case we need to escape the ship during the night."

We searched the ship and soon got hold of enough empty flasks and canisters. Connecting them together, we made life preservers, which we all quickly put on. Fritz and his brothers now slept soundly while Elizabeth and I kept watch all night.
The next morning we gathered on the remaining portion of the deck.
"Where are the sailors?" asked my youngest son, Franz.
"Have they taken away all the boats?" asked Jack.
I nodded gravely.
"The sea will soon be calm enough for swimming," Fritz reassured his younger brothers.
"That's fine for you and Father!" exclaimed Ernest. "But think of Mother and the rest of us! Why not build a raft so we can all go ashore together?"
"It would be difficult to build a raft that would carry us safely," I said. "But let's think about that while we explore the ship to see what might be of use to us."
While I checked on the food and water, my wife took Franz to help her feed the animals on board. Jack went to the captain's cabin. When he opened the door, out sprang two large but friendly dogs!
Back in our cabin we displayed our treasures. Fritz brought a couple of guns, powder flasks, and plenty of bullets. Ernest had nails, a saw, and a hammer while other tools stuck out of his pockets.
"Look at these nice sharp hooks!" said little Franz, proudly showing us a box of fishhooks.
"Well done, Franz!" I said. "Those may save our lives by keeping us fed."
"I have some good news," said my dear wife. "Some useful animals are still alive: a cow, a donkey, two goats, six sheep, and a fine pig."
"Now we just have to figure out how to get ashore," I said.
"Can't we each get into a big tub and float there?" said Jack. "I've often sailed like that around the pond at home."
"A splendid idea!" I said.
We soon found four tall wooden casks floating in the hold. After dragging them on deck, we managed—with some difficulty—to saw them in half.
I was proud of our work, but my wife looked in dismay at the eight tubs. "I'll never get into one of those!" she declared.
"Just wait," I said.
I arranged my tubs in a row, connecting them with planks along the bottom and sides. When I finished, I was confident our boat would be perfectly safe in smooth water.
There was only one problem: Our boat was so heavy that we couldn't move it an inch.
How could we move that heavy boat? I stood on the deck, looking at the wreckage around us.
"We need a lever and rollers!" I cried. "Fetch me a sturdy wooden plank for a lever. We can make rollers from what's left of a mast."

Fritz quickly brought a plank, and I cut up a mast. Then I raised the bow of our boat with the plank while my sons placed a roller under it. We repeated the process, placing two more rollers under the boat. When we once again began to push, we were able to launch our boat into the water.
"Now, my beloved family," I announced, "it's time to make our escape. Leave plenty of food near the animals. Then collect everything that may be of use to us."

The boys joyfully obeyed me. From the large quantity of things they gathered, I chose canvas for a tent, a chest of carpenter's tools, fishing rods, an iron pot, cases of biscuits and dried soup, and some other items.
We now began to take our seats, each one of us in our own tub. Just then we heard the roosters crowing as if scolding us for abandoning them.
"Let's take them with us," urged my wife.
So we placed ten hens and a couple of roosters in one tub with some wire netting over the top. The ducks and geese took to the water at once while the pigeons swiftly flew toward shore.
"This is my contribution," said my wife, throwing a mysterious bag to Franz.

All being ready, we cast off and moved away from the wreck. My good, brave wife sat in the first compartment. Then came Franz, our youngest son, followed by Fritz, our oldest son. The center tubs contained our valuable cargo. Then came our third son, bold Jack, followed by Ernest, our intelligent but rather lazy second son. I stood in the stern, trying to guide the boat to a safe landing place.
We had left the two large dogs, Turk and Juno on the wreck. But when they saw us deserting them, they sprang into the sea after us.

As we neared the shore, it appeared rocky and barren. The geese and ducks, however, found an opening between the rocks where a stream flowed into the sea. I steered after them, and we soon found ourselves in a small, calm bay.

As soon as we could gather our children around us on dry land, we knelt in prayer. Then together we unloaded the boat and set up a tent. The younger boys quickly gathered moss and grass for beds. I made a fireplace with some large flat stones near the brook. Then my wife began making soup with the help of little Franz.
"Mama, don't you want some beef?" he asked as she added water to the dried soup.
"Where can I get it, dear?" she reminded him. "We're a long way from a butcher's shop."
"Oh," he said quietly.

Meanwhile Fritz climbed over the rocks to see what lay beyond the stream. That kind of brisk exercise didn't suit Ernest, so he wandered down to the beach. Jack scrambled among the rocks searching for shellfish.
I was eager to grab two casks that had been floating near our boat. While struggling to do that, I heard Jack cry out.
"Help!" he screamed.
Fearing he was in great danger, I ran and found him standing in a deep pool. A huge lobster had caught his leg in its powerful claw! Poor Jack was very frightened.
"It won't let me go!" he cried.

I grabbed the lobster firmly by the back, and it released its grip. Jack carried the lobster triumphantly to the tent. He urged his mother to add it to the soup, but she decided to save it for another meal.
"Congratulations, Jack," I said. "You're the first to discover something useful."
"I found something good to eat too. Oysters!" said Ernest. "But I didn't want to get my feet wet. And I found sea salt in the crevices of the rocks."
"Never let me hear you object to getting your feet wet," I said. "See how quickly the sun has dried Jack and me."
My wife stirred the soup with a stick. "Our soup is ready, but how will we eat it without bowls or spoons?"
"Oyster shells!" Ernest exclaimed.

The boys ran off to get some oysters. By the time they came back, Fritz had also returned with reports of the beautiful country that lay beyond the stream. We ate the oysters and scooped up our soup with the shells. As the sun set, my wife pulled some oats from her mysterious bag and fed the poultry. Our first day ashore drew peacefully to a close.
The roosters woke me at daybreak, and I then woke my wife. In the quiet interval before the boys were up, we discussed our situation.
"Do you think any sailors reached land?" she asked me.
"I don't know, but we need to find out," I replied. "We also need to learn more about this place where we're stranded."
We decided that Fritz and I would start on an expedition after breakfast. My wife would remain near our landing place with the other boys.

After packing up some food and water, Fritz and I set out. We walked upstream until we reached a waterfall. Then we crossed the stream using several large rocks as stepping stones. On the other side of the stream was a field of tall grass.

We had just begun to force our way through the grass when we heard a rustling sound. Turning around, we saw the grass waving as if some animal were passing through. Fritz brought his gun to his shoulder.
"Turk!" cried Fritz, lowering his gun as the dog approached.
"It's a good thing you didn't fire," I said.

The three of us headed toward the beach to search for any sign of the sailors. We pushed on until we came to a grove of trees stretching down to the water's edge. A thousand brightly colored birds twittered in the branches above. As we gazed up at them, Fritz stumbled over a round object on the ground.
"This must be a bird's nest," he said.
"Every round, hairy thing is not a bird's nest." I laughed. "This is a coconut, and it should be full of delicious liquid."
We split the coconut open, but found that it had dried up.
Moving on, we came to some trees with strange bumps on their trunks.
"Those are calabash trees," I said, recognizing them from travel books. "The bumps are gourds. The natives make bowls, spoons, and bottles from gourds, and even cooking vessels."
"That's impossible!" Fritz pointed out. "A gourd would burn if it were set on the fire."

"The natives don't set the gourd on the fire," I replied. "They cut it in two and hollow it out. Then they fill it with water and food. Next they add red-hot stones until the water boils and the food is done."
"How clever!" said Fritz.

We cut some gourds and left them to pick up on our way home. For three hours we kept walking. At last we came to a piece of land that stretched into the sea. From its rocky summit, I knew we could obtain a good view of the surrounding country.

We reached the top with little difficulty. Before us stretched a wide and lovely bay, and the scene inland was no less beautiful. But both Fritz and I felt lonely as we realized we were the only people there.
"Cheer up, Fritz," I said. "Remember that we chose a settler's life when we left Switzerland, although we didn't expect to be so utterly alone."

We descended the hill and headed toward a clump of palm trees. But to reach them we had to pass through a dense thicket of reeds. Fearing that we might encounter a snake, I broke off a reed for a weapon. I soon noticed liquid dripping from one end. When I tasted it, I realized the reeds were sugarcanes.
"Fritz, we must cut some of these for Mother."

We cut as many as we could carry and continued toward the palm trees. As we emerged from the sugarcane thicket, we spotted a troop of monkeys playing under the palm trees. They quickly climbed to the top of the trees.
"Monkeys are natural mimics," I said. "Watch this."
I gathered some stones and tossed them up toward the monkeys. They instantly seized all the coconuts within reach and tossed them down to us.

Fritz was delighted with my trick and gathered up some of the finest coconuts. These were fresh, so I made some holes in the shells and we enjoyed the delicious liquid inside. Then I cut the coconuts in two and we ate the meat that lined their shells.

It was now time to head home. We walked slowly with our load of sugarcanes and coconuts. Turk bounded ahead of us and surprised another troop of monkeys playing on the ground. They all escaped except for a little one, who tried to hide in the grass.
Fritz rushed to its rescue, flinging away all he was carrying and losing his hat in his haste. With one leap, the monkey was on his shoulders, holding tight to Fritz's thick, curly hair.
"Help!" cried Fritz as he tried to pull the creature off. "Help me, Father!"
Fritz danced and shouted but couldn't pry the baby monkey from his shoulders.
"Stand still," I said. "You're only upsetting him."
I pulled out a biscuit and offered a piece to the monkey, who was no bigger than a kitten.
Finally after some coaxing, I was able to take the monkey into my own arms.
"What a cute little fellow he is!" exclaimed Fritz. "Do let me keep him, Father. I'll call him Knips."
The monkey settled himself on Fritz's shoulder—calmly this time—and I helped to carry Fritz's sugarcane.
But Knips soon scrambled into Fritz's arms, which were already full.
"Come, Turk!" Fritz called, and the dog came quickly to his side. "Now I need you to be a good dog."

Fritz seated Knips on Turk's back and secured the monkey with a cord. Then he put a second cord around Turk's neck so he could lead the dog. At first neither animal was pleased with this arrangement, but they soon got used to it.
We made our way back to camp, where my wife was preparing supper.
"A monkey! A monkey!" cried Franz as he spied the new pet.
"Where did you find him?" asked Ernest.
"Why are you carrying a bundle of sticks? What are those strange nuts?" said Jack as he caught sight of the sugarcane and coconuts.
Over our meal we answered all their questions.
Although Fritz tried to feed Knips, the monkey was not interested in our meal of fish and cheese. But I persuaded Knips to suck liquid from a handkerchief that had been dipped in a coconut.

The next morning I decided that Fritz and I should return to the wreck. Since the ship was meant to supply a colony, there were still many useful things onboard. I wanted to retrieve them before a storm damaged the wreck, and I wanted to check on the animals. Fritz insisted on taking Knips along.
When we boarded the ship, the animals seemed glad to see us.
We checked that they had enough food and then began examining the contents of the ship. We loaded some food and supplies onto our tub boat, but I kept thinking about the animals.
"Fritz, I'm beginning to feel sorry for these poor creatures. I wish there were some way we could get them all ashore."
"We could make a raft and take one or two at a time," he suggested.
"It's easy enough to say 'make a raft,' but it's quite another thing to actually make one," I pointed out.
"Well, I can't think of anything else." Fritz frowned. "Unless we make them life preservers like we made for ourselves."
"That's a good idea!" I exclaimed.
Fritz started to laugh.
"Really, my boy, I'm not joking. We could probably get all the animals ashore that way."
So I found a fat sheep and began to put our plan into action.
First I fastened a wide piece of linen around its belly. Next I attached some corks and empty tins to the linen. Then, with Fritz's help, I dropped the animal into the sea.
It sank! But a moment later, it rose to the surface and floated perfectly.
"Hurrah!" exclaimed Fritz. "We'll make life preservers for all the animals!"

We then quickly caught the other animals and provided them with similar devices. The cow and the donkey gave us more trouble than the others because we needed something more buoyant than cork to help them float. But at last we found some empty casks and fastened two to each animal.

The whole herd was now ready to start, and the donkey was the first to be launched. After some maneuvering, we got him into a good position, and then heaved him into the water. Like the sheep, he sank but immediately surfaced again.

The cow, sheep, and goats followed him, one after another, until only the pig remained. But she seemed determined not to leave the ship. She kicked and squealed so violently that I really thought we would have to abandon her.

Finally after much trouble, we succeeded in launching her. We had fastened a rope to the neck or horns of each animal. Ready to embark, we gathered up the ropes. Then we set sail, pulling our herd behind us. Delighted with the success of our plan, we got out some biscuits for lunch. While Fritz amused himself with Knips, I took out my telescope. I was trying to see what our loved ones were doing onshore when Fritz suddenly shouted.
"Shark!" he cried.
A huge shark was headed straight for one of our finest sheep.
Before I could react, Fritz raised his gun to his shoulder and fired at the shark. The monstrous fish disappeared under the water, and our sheep was safe.
"Well done!" I cried.
Fritz's eyes sparkled at my praise. He carefully watched the water for the shark, but it didn't reappear.
With a breeze in our sail, we quickly reached shore where I released the animals.

My wife and the three younger boys came running to meet us. They helped to collect the animals and unload supplies from our boat. We were hungry, but when we reached camp, there was no sign of supper.
"Fritz and I can supply some ham," I volunteered, pointing to the supplies from the ship.
My wife smiled. "Ernest, let's see if we can conjure up some eggs."
"Where did you get these?" I asked as Ernest proudly set before me a dozen turtle eggs.
"I'll tell you over supper when I describe how we spent our day," said my wife.
Supper consisted of an omelet followed by ham and cheese. After I told the others about our adventures with the animals and shark, my wife began her story.
"The sun beats down on this bare, rocky spot all day," she said. "And it's even hotter inside the tent. I decided that you and Fritz weren't the only ones who could do something for this family."
So she and the boys had set out to find a cooler place to live. Accompanied by the two dogs, they'd crossed the stream and the field of tall grass.
"We soon came to a grove of a dozen trees. I really can't describe how huge and strange they were," my wife continued. "Their roots arched above the ground."
She told how Jack had scrambled up above the roots of one tree and measured its circumference with a piece of string.
"I think it was eighteen yards around!" said Jack.

The spot was shady and cool, and the longer they'd stayed there, the more my wife had liked it. "If only we could live among the branches of those grand, noble trees, I'd feel perfectly safe and happy," she said.
She'd liked the place so much that she didn't feel the need to search anymore. They'd returned home by way of the beach.
"That's where we found the eggs!" said Ernest. "Or I should say, the dogs found them."
Everyone laughed. The boys went off to play while my wife and I continued to talk. "I hope you're in favor of packing everything up and taking us to live among my splendid trees," said Mother.
"So you want us to perch in these trees like birds?" I said. "If we had wings, it would be a wonderful idea."
"My idea is not as silly as you think. A house among the branches would keep us safe from wild animals. And I've seen such a house in Switzerland. I climbed a staircase to reach it."
I was reluctant to leave our current spot, which was protected by high cliffs. But my wife continued to make her argument for a house in the treetops. At last I agreed.
"We'll have to build a bridge first," I said, "in order to carry everything across the stream."
"A bridge!" she exclaimed. "I'll die from the heat if I have to wait for a bridge."
"We'll need bags and baskets to carry everything," I said. "If you focus on those, I promise the boys and I will make a bridge as quickly as possible."

So the next day everyone set to work. Using planks that had washed up from the wreck, we soon completed our bridge. When moving day arrived, everyone was busy. Some collected provisions. Others packed kitchen utensils and tools into baskets tied onto the cow and donkey. We planned to return later for the ducks and geese.
"Leave room for Franz to ride on the donkey!" my wife called out. "Oh! I almost forgot the chickens and pigeons!"

Away ran the boys to catch the chickens and pigeons. The result was a lot of chasing, fluttering, cackling, and cooing. But they didn't catch any of them. At last my wife scattered some grain inside the tent. Lured by the food, the chickens and pigeons were easily caught, tied together, and placed on the cow's back.

And off we went! Fritz and my wife led the caravan. Then came Franz on the donkey, followed by the cow. Jack led the goats with Knips riding one of them. Ernest was in charge of the sheep. I brought up the rear while the two dogs raced back and forth. Meanwhile the pig stubbornly refused to join us.
We had just crossed the bridge when I heard the pig grunting and squealing angrily behind us. She had decided to come with us after all, but she clearly wasn't happy about it.
When we reached the grove of trees, I was amazed by the trees' great size and unusual appearance.
"A house up there will be the safest and most charming home in the world," I said.
"I knew you'd like it," said my wife. "Now I think we should prepare a meal."
Ernest started fetching large, flat stones for a fireplace while Franz gathered wood.
"What kind of trees do you think these are?" asked Ernest.
"They must be mangroves or wild figs. I've heard of their great height and strange curving roots," I replied.
Just then little Franz came up with a large bundle of sticks. He was happily chewing something.
"Oh, Mother, this is so good!" he said.
"What are you eating?" she cried in alarm. "It's probably poisonous. Spit it out right now!"
"Where did you find this?" I bent down and saw what appeared to be a half-chewed fig.
"There are thousands of them in the grass over there," said Franz.
"These do appear to be fig trees, but you must never eat anything without showing it to me first. Promise?" I asked him.
Franz nodded in agreement.

After we ate, our first task was to make a rope ladder with wood steps. The older boys and I went to the beach to gather wood while Franz stayed behind with my wife. She started making harnesses for the cow and donkey.
We soon had the ladder fastened securely to the tree above and the ground below.
"I want to climb up first!" cried Jack. "Please, Father."
"No, Father," said Ernest. "I should because—"
"I'm the oldest," Fritz interrupted him to remind us.
"Jack will have the honor," I said, "because he asked so nicely."
Jack quickly sprang to the top of the ladder. "Three cheers for the nest!" he exclaimed.
I gave Fritz a rope to take up, and then Ernest and I followed him on the ladder.
"Send up the pulley," I called to my wife as I dangled the rope next to the ladder.
She tied the pulley to the rope, and I hauled it up. Then I fastened it to a branch overhead so it would be ready for the next day's work.

We awoke early the next morning. My wife milked the goats and cow while the boys and I fed the animals. After that we went down to the beach to collect more wood for our house. We harnessed the cow and donkey to the larger beams and dragged the rest ourselves.

Fritz and I then climbed the tree to finish the preparations. We cut many branches to clear a living space. But we left a few on which to hang our hammocks. Higher up, we kept some branches to support a sailcloth roof.

My wife fastened the boards to the rope, and I used the pulley to haul them up. Fritz and I arranged the boards to make a smooth, solid floor. Then we built two walls. Our house was now enclosed on three sides because the great trunk formed a wall behind us. We left the front open to let in the fresh sea breeze. After attaching the sailcloth roof, our next job was to haul up our hammocks and hang them.

We had been working all day, but a few hours of sunlight remained. Using the last of the wood, we made a table and benches. Finally Fritz and I, exhausted, threw ourselves on the grass. My wife arranged supper on our new table.
We were just finishing supper when the pig appeared. My wife gave it all the milk that was left.
"The milk will be sour before morning in this heat," she said.
"You're right," I said. "The next time Fritz and I visit the wreck, we'll try to bring back a butter churn."
"Must you really return to that dreadful wreck?" My wife shuddered. "You have no idea how anxious I am when you're there."
"We must go back, but not tomorrow," I told her. "Come, it's getting late. Time for sleep."

We lit our watch fires to keep away any wild animals. Fritz, Ernest, and Jack climbed up the ladder in a moment. Mother followed very cautiously. Although she had wanted to build this nest, she hesitated at the idea of sleeping so far off the ground.

When she was safely in the house, I took little Franz on my back. I released the fasteners that held the lower end of the ladder to the ground. With the ladder swinging to and fro, we slowly went up, leaving the dogs below.

7.title: A Quiet Sunday and a Busy Monday

paragraphs.text: The next morning everyone was awake early. The children sprang about the tree house like monkeys while I sat beneath the great tree.
"What should we do next, Father?" Franz called down to me. "What do you want us to do today?"
"Rest, my boys," I replied. "Rest."
"Rest?" Franz repeated. "Why should we rest?"
"It's Sunday. Come down here, please."

"Is it really Sunday?" asked Jack when he'd climbed down the ladder. "How jolly! I won't do any work. I'll take a bow and arrow and prowl through the woods. And we'll climb about the tree and have fun all day."
"That's not resting, Jack," I pointed out. "That's not the way you usually spend Sundays."
"I usually go to church, but we don't have a church here."
"And we don't have a clergyman or an organ," added little Franz.
"We can still offer thanks for our new home," I said. "Come, everyone, gather around me."

After I led my family in some prayers and hymns, the boys were free to do as they liked. I continued to sit under our tree. A few birds came to feed on the figs, which were just beginning to ripen. I realized that as more figs ripened, more birds would come. If we could preserve some birds, we could eat them during the rainy season when food might be scarce.
Relieved that I'd thought of a way to provide food for my family, I enjoyed my morning in the shade. During lunch I proposed that we name all the places we'd visited since we arrived.
"We'll feel more at home if these places have names," I said. "Let's start by naming the bay where we landed."
"Oyster Bay," said Fritz.
"No, no," protested Jack. "Lobster Bay, in memory of the fellow who grabbed my leg."
"I think we should call it Safety Bay," said my wife. "It will be a token of our gratitude for a safe escape from the ship."
"I like it!" said Ernest.

The others agreed, and so the bay was known as Safety Bay from that moment on. We easily decided on Tentholm for the place where we first lived. Many names were proposed for our tree house, but we finally decided on Falconhurst.

We spent the rest of the day quietly. The following morning I proposed an expedition to Tentholm. We went by a different route. The boys roamed ahead of my wife and me. Knips the monkey rode along on Juno the dog. Soon I heard a joyful shout, and Ernest came running toward me at full speed, followed by his brothers. He held out a plant for me to see.
"Potatoes! Potatoes, Father!" Ernest was gasping for breath.
"Yes," said Jack. "Acres and acres of potatoes. Come look at them."
My wife and I hurried to the spot. There indeed was a great area of land covered with potato plants.
"Ernest, you've made a great discovery," I said. "With all these potatoes, we'll always have something to eat."
"Ernest may have the honor of discovering the potatoes," said Jack. "But I'll have the honor of being the first to harvest them."

So he set to work digging potatoes with his hands. Knips followed his example and soon had a pile of potatoes beside him. Everyone began digging, and we didn't stop until we'd filled every bag, pouch, and pocket.

We pushed on to Tentholm, loaded down with potatoes but happy with our find. Along the way the boys pestered me for the names and uses of the many strange plants and trees we passed. I recognized some of them, but there were many others that I couldn't identify.

Everything was safe at Tentholm, and we began gathering what we wanted to take back. I collected a fresh supply of salt, and my wife wanted to make butter. Jack and Ernest ran down to the beach to capture the geese and ducks that we'd left behind. The birds were out on the water, and nothing could persuade them to come ashore.
"I know!" said Ernest. "Let's ask Mother for some cheese and string."
"Cheese and string?" said Jack. "Who will eat that?"
"Just watch," said Ernest as he led Jack to the tent for supplies.

Back at the beach, the boys broke off pieces of cheese and tied a long string around each one. Ernest threw the bait into the water, and the hungry birds instantly went after it. With a little maneuvering, he got the birds onshore, where Jack caught them and tied their feet together.
We soon set off for Falconhurst. After a pleasant walk, we were back at our tree house. I released the birds into our stream. After a delicious supper of potatoes, milk, and butter, we went to bed.

After breakfast the next morning, it was time to make another trip to the wreck with Fritz. I called Ernest and Jack because I wanted to give them some instructions before we left. But they had disappeared.
"We're in need of potatoes," said my wife. "I guess they went to dig some up."

"When they come back," I said, "you must scold them for leaving without telling us where they were going. They seem to have taken Turk along, so I suppose no harm will come to them. But they still shouldn't have gone without our permission."
I was reluctant to leave my dear wife alone with little Franz. And she was never happy when we visited the wreck. But I promised her we would be careful.
"We'll be back tomorrow," I called over my shoulder as we set out.
We had just crossed the bridge when suddenly Jack and Ernest burst out of their hiding place.
"Surprise!" cried Ernest.
"We're coming with you!" announced Jack.
The two boys danced with delight at having fooled their older brother and me.
"No, you must go back and take care of Mother and Franz," I said firmly.
"Oh, Father, please may we come?" begged Ernest.
"It'll be an adventure," said Jack.
I couldn't let them come with us. The wreck might be dangerous, and we needed to get some work done. But I also couldn't find it in my heart to scold the two merry rascals.
"Hurry home so Mother won't worry about you," I said.

Fritz and I waited a few minutes to be sure the boys were really heading home. Then we finished our hike to Safety Bay, where we found our tub boat. The current carried us briskly out of the bay, and we were soon moored alongside the wreck. We scrambled on deck and began to make our plans.
"We need to build a raft to carry things that are too large for the tub boat," I said.
"Let's use these empty water casks," said Fritz. "There must be a dozen of them."

We tightly closed the casks, pushed them overboard, and arranged them in rows of three. After securing the casks together with pieces of wood, we built a deck of planks. Building the raft took us all day.
We made an excellent supper from the ship's provisions and then went to bed. That night we slept on thick, soft mattresses—a luxury after our hammocks.

The next morning Fritz and I began loading the raft and tub boat. We first carried off the entire contents of our own cabins, including those wonderful mattresses. From the captain's cabin, we removed the furniture as well as the doors and window frames. We then took the chests belonging to the ship's officers, carpenter, and gunsmith.
"Look at this!" cried Fritz as he opened another chest filled with gold and silver watches, buckles, chains, and rings. "It's like a jeweler's shop."

We also found a box of money, but that was of no use to us now. Of more interest was a group of young fruit trees: apple, pear, peach, cherry. There were plumber's tools, paint, cart wheels, sacks of peas, oats, and wheat. We even spotted all the parts of a sawmill, carefully numbered so that they could be put back together.
We were so bewildered by the wealth around us that we couldn't decide what to take with us.
"We can't take everything," I said.
"Yes, Father," Fritz agreed. "But the first storm will destroy the wreck, and we'll lose anything we leave behind."
Fritz was right. We made our choices, and our haul included fishing lines, reels, rope, and a mariner's compass. Remembering our encounter with the shark, Fritz insisted that we take a harpoon.

Early in the afternoon both our vessels were heavily loaded, and we were ready to set sail. With the raft in tow, I was anxious that we might tip over. But the sea was calm and the wind was favorable. We spread our sail and soon neared shore.
Fritz fired his gun to signal our arrival and not long after, the whole family arrived on the beach. We unloaded the raft and tub boat and began to carry some things back to Falconhurst.

When we arrived, Ernest was eager to show me some plants that he'd dug up. "I don't know what they are," he said. "I didn't dare to taste them even though the pig was devouring them as fast as she could."
"That was a wise decision," I said.
Ernest brought me some of the plants, and I examined them thoroughly. "Why, Ernest, I believe you've made a brilliant discovery!"
After carefully examining what Ernest had found, I determined that they were cassava plants. With the plants' roots, we could lose every other food that we possessed and still not go hungry.

"If we can collect enough roots," I said, "we'll attempt to make bread. But the plant can be poisonous. We'll need to take great care in preparing the flour and baking the bread. First we must finish unloading the tub boat and the raft."

That job took us the rest of the afternoon and part of the next morning. I had intended to spend the rest of the day at Falconhurst. But the sea was calm, so I decided to make another trip to the wreck. Ernest and Franz returned to the tree house with my wife while Jack lingered on the beach.
"You want to go with us, don't you?" I said to him. "Well, come on then."
Jack grinned and quickly followed Fritz and me onto the tub boat. When we reached the wreck, Jack went down into the hold. I soon heard a loud rattling noise as he joined me on deck.
"Look what I found—a wheelbarrow!" he said. "This is just the thing for bringing home potatoes."
He was then followed by Fritz, who had made an even more important discovery.
"I found a small sailboat!" he announced. "All the parts are packed together. There are even a couple of small brass cannons!"
If he was right, then this would be a most useful item. I hurried to look at the sailboat.
"Oh," I said with disappointment in my voice.

Yes, it was a sailboat. But it was going to take a lot of work to put it together and make it seaworthy. At the moment we only had time enough to get something to eat and hurry to the tub boat. We carried home a copper boiler, iron plates, tobacco graters, and three wheelbarrows.
At Falconhurst my wife and the other boys had gathered a large supply of potatoes and cassava roots. I praised them lavishly.
"Oh, Father!" blurted out little Franz. "What will you say when Mother and I give you melons and pumpkins and cucumbers?"
"You little chatterbox," my wife said fondly. "You've let out my secret! I wanted to surprise Father when my plants sprouted."
I was puzzled. "Where did you get the seeds?"
"From my bag, of course," she replied. "Every time I've gone for potatoes, I've sown seeds in the ground that we've dug up. I've also planted potatoes."
My wife looked very pleased. But then she caught sight of the tobacco graters that we'd brought from the wreck.
"You aren't going to make snuff?" she said in alarm.
"No," I said. "Please treat my graters with respect because they'll provide you with fresh bread."
"What connection can there be between tobacco graters and bread?" asked my wife. "Besides, you need an oven to bake bread, and we don't have one."
"You can't expect real loaves," I said. "But I think I can bake flat cakes on these iron plates. We'll have to make flour first."
My wife looked skeptical. "It's probably a good thing we dug potatoes today."

After thoroughly washing the cassava roots, I spread a large sailcloth on the ground. Then I called the boys and gave them each a tobacco grater. Everyone worked at grating down the roots. Luckily, no one was tempted to stop and taste the flour because it looked like wet sawdust.

When we were finished, we put the damp flour in a canvas bag. I squeezed and squeezed, but the flour was still wet. We laid the canvas bag on a board and put another board over it. Then we found the heaviest things we owned—an anvil, iron bars—and set them on the top board. The pressure on the bag was enormous, and the liquid flowed from it to the ground.
"Could we bake some bread now?" asked Fritz. "There doesn't seem to be any moisture left."
"Certainly, but I will make only a small sample today. We must first see how it agrees with Knips and the hens."
I placed an iron plate over the fire. While it was getting hot, I mixed the flour with water and salt. After kneading the dough, I laid it on the hot plate to bake.
The cake smelled delicious! I gave a small amount to the monkey and two hens. We watched them all evening for any signs of poisoning.

The next morning the animals were fine, so we baked more bread. Each boy busily prepared his own cake. Some of the bread was burned; some was underdone. But much of it was golden brown. We were soon enjoying a delicious breakfast of bread and milk.

Having provided bread for my family, I began to think again about the wreck and all the valuables on board. Most of all I wanted to acquire the beautiful little sailboat. But I knew I would need a lot of help to do so.
I began to coax my wife to let me take all the boys except Franz.
"I'll consent to this," she finally said, "but you must promise me one thing."
"Anything," I said eagerly.
"You'll never spend another night on that dangerous wreck."
"I promise."
The three boys were delighted to go along. At Safety Bay we fastened on our life preservers and stepped into the tub boat. With the raft in tow, we steered straight for the wreck.

On board I directed the boys to collect some provisions and load the raft. Meanwhile I studied the sailboat parts, which were stowed in a small compartment in the hold. The space was so narrow that it would be impossible to put the pieces together there. But the individual parts were so heavy that we couldn't move them to a bigger space.
"Room to work in, boys! That's what we need first," I said when they came to see what I was doing. "Fetch axes and let's break down the walls around the sailboat."

We worked hard, but as evening approached, we'd made little progress. Leaving the wreck, we headed for Safety Bay. Imagine our surprise when we found my wife and Franz waiting for us at Tentholm. She had decided to live there while we worked on the wreck.
"That way you'll live nearer your work, and I won't lose sight of you," she said.
I was delighted by her plan. "We'll work with great speed, so you may soon return to your beloved Falconhurst."
We spent our days clearing an open space around the sailboat. Then we worked on putting the parts together. We started early and returned at night, always bringing valuable cargo from the old wreck.

At last the sailboat was ready to be launched. But it was still imprisoned within massive wooden walls. We had been able to free the boat from its compartment, but we couldn't break through the ship's hull.
Now it seemed that our work would end in failure and disappointment. I was almost in despair when an idea suddenly came to me.

I took a large cannon, filled it with gunpowder, and added a long fuse. Then I placed the cannon so that it would blow out the side of the ship when it exploded. After the boys were in the tub boat, I lit the fuse. My heart was pounding as I hurried after them.
We sailed back to Safety Bay, where we began unloading the day's haul. No one noticed my anxiety as I waited for the sound of the explosion. And then it came—a mighty roar! A grand burst of smoke!
Terror-stricken, my wife and children looked first toward the sea and then at me.
"Perhaps you left a light burning near some gunpowder," suggested my wife.
"That's possible," I said quietly. "I'll go see what's happened. Will anyone come with me?"

The boys sprang into the tub boat. The wreck looked the same from the side where we usually approached. But then we pulled around to the other side. There was a huge hole in the side of the ship, and the decks were torn apart.
"Hurrah!" I cried. "The sailboat is ours!"
The boys looked at me in surprise.
"You planned that explosion!" said Ernest.
"Yes, I did," I admitted. "But let's not tell Mother or Franz. I want them to be surprised when we sail into the bay."

I had put rollers beneath the sailboat before the explosion. So with levers and pulleys we were able to gently lower the boat into the water. The boys spent the next few days helping me rig the boat and mount the two little brass cannons.

Casting off from the wreck and spreading our sail, we began our voyage. The sailboat glided swiftly through the water. I stood at the helm. Ernest and Jack manned the cannons while Fritz gave the signal.
"Fire!" he cried.
Bang! Bang! The sound of the cannons echoed among the cliffs, followed by our happy shouts.
My wife and Franz greeted us onshore. Fritz helped them to come aboard.
"I don't know whether to scold you or praise you," said Mother breathlessly. "First I was startled by the sight of this strange boat. Then I heard the cannons. If I hadn't recognized your shouts—"
"But do you like our sailboat?" interrupted Jack.
"I do indeed, you dear, horrid, wonderful boys." My wife gave Jack a hug. "But don't you ever scare me like that again!"
One day while Fritz and I were out exploring, I noticed some interesting bushes. They were loaded with small, white berries that were waxy in appearance.
"You know, Fritz, we might be able to use these berries to make candles," I said.
"Oh, that would make Mother happy. She doesn't like having to set aside her work and go to bed as soon as the sun sets."

The wax would be more brittle than beeswax, but it would burn well and with a pleasant scent. Having the donkey with us, we quickly gathered enough berries to fill one of the large canvas sacks he carried.

We then continued on our way. Very soon we came upon a tree with a whole colony of birds. Their nests were built in a mass around the tree trunk and branches. A roof-like covering of straw and grass protected the colony from the rain and hot sun.
"The nests are like rooms in a house!" said Fritz.
We watched as the birds swarmed in and out by the thousands. Most of them were plain brown birds, but there were also a few beautiful, bright parakeets.
Fritz was curious about the nests so he climbed the tree. He put his hands into several nests, hoping to capture a young bird.
"Ow!" he cried. "Something pecked my finger."
He reached back in and pulled out a small bird. Fritz's prize was not one of the brown birds, but a pretty green parakeet. For the moment he put it in his pocket and we walked on.
Our next discovery was a strange tree with bark that oozed a gummy resin. Fritz scraped some off.
"Look at this, Father. When I stretch this gum, it springs right back. Do you think it could be rubber?"
"If it is, that's a most valuable discovery."
"Why is it valuable? I've only seen rubber used for erasing pencil marks. How else can you use it?"
"I would try to make waterproof boots and shoes!"
Pleased with our discoveries, we headed back to Falconhurst.

The next morning the boys wanted to make candles as soon as breakfast was over. We put the berries in a large, shallow iron pot on the fire. The sweet-scented wax melted rapidly. We skimmed it from the surface of the berry juice, and put it in another pot. I then took the wicks my wife had prepared and dipped them in the wax.
"These are very skinny candles," said Ernest as the boys hung them on a bush to dry.
"They're not done yet," I said. "We're going to dip them several times."
We soon had sturdy candles, which we left in a cool spot to harden. And that night Falconhurst was brilliantly illuminated for the first time.

"You are very clever indeed," my wife said to me. "I just wish you could figure out a way to make butter. Day after day I'm annoyed about the large amount of good cream that goes bad before I can use it."
"Let me think about that. I hoped we would find a churn on the wreck, but we didn't."
By the next morning, I had come up with a plan. "Bring me one of our gourd bottles," I said to Jack.
He quickly fetched a gourd that we had hollowed out. We had also added a small hole at one end. I partially filled the gourd with cream and then tightly plugged the hole with a piece of cork.
"Here, boys," I said. "You can continue the job while I become a carpenter and build a cart."

I gave them some directions and set about my own work. The boys pounded four stakes into the ground. Then they fastened a square of sailcloth to the stakes with cord. After that they placed the gourd full of cream on this cloth cradle. Each taking a side of the cloth, they rolled the gourd back and forth without stopping.
"This is hard work," complained Ernest.
"No it isn't," said Jack. "This is fun."
"Keep at it, boys," I said as I looked up from my work. "This is going to take a while."
I expected little Franz to complain too. But he was just happy to be helping his older brothers with some real and useful work.
After half an hour I told the boys to stop and look inside the gourd.
"What's happened to the cream?" asked little Franz, shaking the gourd.
"We've turned it into butter!" said Jack.
"Now take the contents to your mother with my compliments," I said.
My wife was delighted with the results from my gourd "churn." That night at supper we had plenty of butter to go with our meal.
"You've more than made up for scaring me with that sailboat!" she said.

Six weeks passed while we worked hard. We planted fruit trees at Falconhurst. After that we worked at Tentholm. I wanted to make it safe in case of emergency. First we planted a thick, prickly hedge that would protect us from wild animals. Then we mounted two cannons from the wreck on a hill above the bay.

The boys were growing strong as I encouraged them to run, climb, and swim. For fun, I also taught them how to use a lasso, and Jack took his everywhere. But all this work and play was wearing out their clothes.

Therefore I decided to pay another visit to the wreck to replenish our wardrobes. I also wanted to see how much longer the vessel was likely to hold together. Luckily there hadn't been a storm yet. The three older boys and I set off in the sailboat.
"Come, boys," I said. "Don't leave behind a single item of the slightest value. Search the ship to the bottom of its hold."

The boys scattered throughout the ship. Soon everything from bales of cloth to window shutters lay in a heap on the deck. We loaded the sailboat and went onshore. After a few more trips, nothing remained.
"I left two barrels of gunpowder on board and lit a very long fuse," I said to my wife when we returned to Tentholm.
That night we ate supper at a spot from which we could see the wreck. Suddenly a vivid pillar of fire rose from the black waters.
"That's the end of the brave ship that carried us from Switzerland," I said softly.

We had planned the destruction of the ship, but we went to bed that night feeling sad. We felt as if we'd lost a dear friend. The next morning we found the shore lined with a rich supply of wood. Our ship had been good to us until the end.
Meanwhile Fritz and I had been planning another expedition into the countryside surrounding Falconhurst.
"Why does Fritz always get to go?" complained Jack.
"Yes," said my wife. "I'd like to see what's beyond Falconhurst too."

So the next morning the whole family started off in our cart pulled by the cow and donkey. We took everything necessary for an expedition of several days. On the first day we gathered more berries to make candles and tapped the rubber trees for their gummy sap. After pitching our tent, we were enjoying supper when our donkey, Grizzle, let out a loud bray.
"What's wrong with him?" asked little Franz as the donkey galloped away.
"I have no idea," I replied, "but we can't afford to lose such a valuable animal."

We followed the donkey for a short distance, but had to give up because it was getting dark. The next morning I took Jack and the dogs with me. We followed Grizzle's tracks in the soil until they mingled with those of other animals. At last we reached a wide plain, and I saw a herd of large animals. Buffalo!
Turk and Juno saw them too and dashed forward before I could stop them. The dogs surrounded a young buffalo, causing the rest of the herd to attack. I fired my gun in the air, and the herd retreated.
"If we could capture that little buffalo, we might train him to work for us," I said.
"I know what to do!" said Jack.

He pulled out his lasso and, twirling it in the air, caught the buffalo by the hind legs. We fastened a rope around the buffalo's neck. With the dogs herding it from either side, we managed to get the buffalo to walk with us.

I decided to give up our donkey search for the moment and return to camp. Juno dashed ahead and was about to rush into a little cave. Suddenly a large jackal sprang out at her. Turk joined the fight, and the two dogs managed to drive off the jackal.
Jack peered inside the cave. "Baby jackals! Oh, Father, may I take one home?"
I glanced around nervously. "Hurry up before the parents come back."
Jack went into the cave and emerged with a yellow cub the size of a cat. He was eager to show his new pet to his brothers.
"Look what I found!" he said triumphantly when we arrived back at our tent.
"And look what I found!" said Fritz, showing us a small eagle.

"Now, boys," I said. "You're collecting a lot of pets. It's not your mother's job to take care of them. You must each look after your own, and if I find any animal neglected, I will set it free. Do you understand?"
The boys nodded solemnly while my wife looked quite relieved.
We had made many improvements to our homes at Falconhurst and Tentholm. But there was one more improvement that my wife wanted us to make at Falconhurst.
"I think that our nest in the tree is perfect," she said. "But I'd like to be able to reach it without climbing that dreadful ladder. Can you build a flight of steps?"

"We might be able to build a staircase inside the trunk of the tree," I replied. "I've often suspected that the trunk is hollow. Didn't you say that you've noticed bees coming from a hole in the tree?"
Before my wife could reply, little Franz piped up. "Oh yes! I went to look at them, and one stung me. I almost cried but I didn't."
"Brave boy!" I said. "Let's see if the tree is really hollow."

Led by Jack, the boys were soon peeping into the hole. They tapped the tree to see if it sounded hollow. In their eagerness they forgot who lived in the tree. The bees, disturbed by all this activity, swarmed out and attacked the boys.
"Ow! Ow! Ow!" cried Jack.
"Nasty bees!" said Fritz as he tried to swat them away.

My wife and I pulled the boys away from the angry bees. They had all been stung on their hands and faces. Before we built a staircase, we removed the bees to a new nesting place in a large gourd. We made good use of the honey and wax that they left behind in the tree.

Then we began working on the stairs. At the base of the tree, we made an opening for a door. We attached a door we'd taken earlier from the captain's cabin. Next we cleared out the rotted wood from the center of the trunk and put up a stout sapling to provide a center pole. With planks from the wreck, we then fashioned steps. As we worked, we cut windows in the trunk for light and air. When we reached the top of the center pole, we added another sapling to reach the floor of our home above. We even included two handrails!

This task took us a whole month, during which we also had to care for our animals. By now several of the goats and sheep had produced offspring. To keep these frisky youngsters from straying, we tied bells around their necks. Juno produced a fine litter of puppies. Jack introduced his little jackal, Fangs, to the litter, and, to his delight, Juno adopted the wild dog.

The other pets were also flourishing and learning new tasks. After giving us much trouble, Storm, the buffalo, was now capable of carrying both people and things. Fritz was so busy teaching his eagle, Pounce, to hunt live prey that he gave Knips to Ernest.

Knips was not allowed to remain idle, as Ernest decided that he should be taught to do something useful. He and Jack made a small basket that fit on the monkey's back. Then Ernest taught Knips to climb coconut and other tall trees and to bring down the fruit in the basket. Jack tried to teach Fangs to retrieve, but the jackal kept eating everything it caught.

Meanwhile I was determined to have some waterproof boots before the start of the rainy season. To make a mold, I filled a pair of socks with sand and coated them with a thin layer of clay. Then I brushed on several layers of rubber. When that had dried, I broke the mold and added some buffalo-hide soles.
"These are wonderful!" said Fritz as he tried on my boots. "Can you make me a pair?"
"Me too!" cried all the other boys.
I was delighted to fill their orders, and soon everyone in the family had a pair of comfortable, durable waterproof boots.

The boys had long been complaining about having to walk to the stream and bring back heavy buckets of water. So our next job was to build a dam with a series of pipes to carry the water to Falconhurst.
One day, as we were finishing this task, we were startled by the roaring or bellowing of a wild beast. The sound was so strange that I couldn't imagine what animal had made it.
"Perhaps it's a lion," offered Jack.
"No, a gorilla," said Fritz.
"More likely a hyena," said Ernest.
"Whatever it is," I said, "we must be ready when it arrives. All of you, hurry to the nest while I secure the door."
I left the dogs outside to protect our animals, closed the door, and joined my family. Every eye was on watch. Every gun was loaded. The dreadful sound came nearer.
The wild animal was silent. My family looked down anxiously from our nest in the treetop.
"Come, Fritz," I whispered. "We must go down and find out what was making that awful noise."

We picked up our guns, and he followed me down the steps. Outside we glided carefully from tree to tree. Suddenly we heard that awful sound again, and it was quite nearby! Fritz raised his gun, but quickly lowered it.
"It's only Grizzle." He laughed as our missing donkey appeared before us.
Our friend was not alone. Behind him trotted another animal resembling a donkey, but slim and graceful as a horse.
"That's a wild donkey, Fritz," I whispered. "Creep back to Falconhurst and bring me two pieces of rope."

He soon returned with the rope and some oats. The wild donkey followed Grizzle's lead and nibbled some oats. I quickly threw the rope around her neck while Fritz captured Grizzle. Despite the wild donkey's kicking and struggling, I managed to lead her back to Falconhurst. We tied both animals under the roots of our tree for the night.

The next morning I realized that we needed to provide better shelter for our animals and ourselves before the rainy season arrived. In addition to our new donkey—which we named Lightfoot—three broods of chickens had recently hatched.

We began by constructing walls and a roof over the roots of our tree. After fastening bamboo canes tightly together, we filled any holes with clay and moss. Then we coated the roof and walls with tar to make everything waterproof. I divided the space into rooms. Stables, henhouse, kitchen, and dining room were soon all under one roof.

Every day we loaded our cart with provisions for our winter quarters: cassava, potatoes, coconuts, and other foods. One day when we were out gathering nuts, Ernest found a nest made from long, broad grass.
"I'll take some of this grass home for Franz," said Ernest, waving a piece around. "He can pretend it's a sword."
When we arrived home, Franz was delighted with his new toy. But Mother was even happier.
"That's not grass," she said. "That's flax. Once it's properly prepared, I can make linen for clothing."
So we added soaking the flax in water to our tasks.

Soon the rain began to fall, and we had to retreat to our shelter under the roots. We carried down any furniture or household items that might be damaged by the moisture. With our beds all around us, our dwelling was crowded indeed.

We gradually rearranged our things so that we had more room. During the day we sent our formerly wild animals outside. We figured that they were used to surviving the rainy season. Every night Fritz and I went outside to bring them back in. And every night we returned home soaked to the skin.
"You need waterproof suits," said my wife. "Let me make some for you."
First she sewed a hood to a heavy shirt. Then she attached the shirt to some pants. She coated the whole outfit with layers of rubber to produce a wonderful waterproof suit.

Time dragged despite our efforts to keep busy. Our days were occupied with caring for our animals and doing chores. In the evenings I wrote in my journal while my wife sewed. Ernest made sketches of the birds, animals, and flowers that he had encountered since our arrival. Fritz and Jack taught little Franz to read.
At last the rainy season was over. We climbed up to our nest and found it filled with broken branches.
"Is Falconhurst ruined?" cried Franz.
"No, no, my boy," I reassured him. "There's nothing here that a few days of hard work can't fix."

I was more worried about Tentholm. And sure enough we found that the tent was blown down and the canvas torn to rags. Our provisions were soaked, and two kegs of gunpowder were ruined. The sailboat was safe, but the tub boat had been destroyed by the waves.
"We need to find a better place to spend the rainy season," I said to Fritz.
He looked at the rocky cliffs surrounding Tentholm. "Maybe we could hollow out a cave in the rock."
A few days later we loaded up our cart with hammers, chisels, pickaxes, and crowbars. The three older boys and I battered away at the rock without making much progress.
But on the tenth day, Jack suddenly shouted, "I lost my crowbar! It fell through a hole and I heard it crash down inside!"
We rushed to his side. "There must be a cavern in there," I said.
With a shout of joy, the boys attacked the rock. And soon the hole was large enough for us to enter the cave.

15.title: Turning a Cave into a Home

paragraphs.text: "Fetch your mother, Jack," I said as we stood at the mouth of the dark cave. "And bring as many candles as you can. We'll need some light to explore this place."
Jack jumped into the cart and urged Storm, the buffalo, to hurry. He soon returned with my wife, Franz, and the two dogs. Everyone was excited about our discovery.
"Are we really going to live here?" asked Franz. "Where will I sleep?"
"How big is this cave?" asked my wife.
"Let's light some candles and find out," I replied.

With our candles lit, we entered the cave and everyone fell silent. The vast cave was like a crystal palace. The candles cast a golden light on the walls, which sparkled like stars. Great crystal pillars rose from the floor and hung from the ceiling.
"What are these crystals?" asked Ernest.
"Rock salt," I said. "And look at the floor. It's made of hard, dry sand. We can live here without the slightest fear of getting wet during the rainy season."

We returned to Falconhurst with our minds full of wonder at our discovery. All we talked about was our new house. Our nest in the tree had seemed so safe and comfortable compared to Tentholm. But now we decided to keep Falconhurst only as a summer residence.

So we set to work on the cave, which we named Rockburg. The first thing was to provide light and air. We cut openings in the rock, and fit them with a door and some windows we'd brought from the ship.

Then we divided the cave into rooms. Our living space included areas for sitting, eating, and sleeping. To the right were our kitchen and workshop. To the left were the stables. Behind all this, in the dark recess of the cave, was our storage area.

We had learned from the last rainy season that we needed to have a proper fireplace and chimney. Our stable arrangements were much better this time too. And there was plenty of space in our workshop for the biggest project.

During this time we made frequent trips to Tentholm. The shore provided us with plenty to eat: lobsters, crabs, and mussels. But one morning there was an additional surprise for us. The sea rolled and heaved, and rays from the sun lit up the water as if it were on fire.
"The sea is boiling!" exclaimed Jack.
"Why are there flashes of silver in the water?" asked Ernest.
"And what are those birds doing?" said Fritz.
Hovering over the water, hundreds of birds were screaming loudly. Then they dove toward the water. Meanwhile a shining, sparkling silver mass in the water rolled directly toward our shore.
"That's a shoal of herring," I said. "Millions of these fish swim together. Pursued by larger fish, they make for shallow waters near the shore. And that's where we'll catch them."

We soon had a fishery in operation. Jack and Fritz stood in the water with baskets and scooped up the fish. After cleaning the fish, Ernest and I preserved them in barrels with layers of salt. When the barrels were full, we rolled them away to the cool storage room at the back of our cave. Now we had not only a place to live during the rainy season, but also some more food.

And our good fortune did not end with the herring. About a month later, Jack spied another shoal of fish. I ran down to the shore with him and realized that these big fish were sturgeon. Jack was delighted with his discovery.
"These are proper fish!" he exclaimed. "Not like those puny herring. How do you preserve these fish—salted or smoked?"
"Not so fast," I replied. "Tell me how you're going to catch them, and I'll tell you how to preserve them."
"Oh, I'll catch them soon enough," he replied.

He darted off to Rockburg and returned with a bow and arrow and a ball of string. After tying the string to the arrow, he advanced to the water's edge. His arrow flew from the bow, and to my surprise struck one of the largest fish.
"Help! Father, help!" cried Jack as the fish darted away with the arrow. "Help! Or he will pull me into the water!"

I ran to his side and together we struggled with the huge fish. As soon as we landed it, Fritz and Ernest appeared. Eager to participate, they rushed off for fishing equipment. They returned and were soon in the water, Fritz with a harpoon and Ernest with a fishing rod.
After some time Fritz managed to harpoon a gigantic sturgeon. But he couldn't land it even with our help.
"I'd hate to lose this fish." He panted. "It must be eight feet long."

16.title: A Day of Thanksgiving and Sports

paragraphs.text: My wife had been watching Fritz try to catch the giant sturgeon. "The buffalo!" she cried suddenly. "Harness him to the harpoon rope, and you'll land that fish!"

Jack ran off to fetch Storm, and we soon captured the sturgeon. When we'd caught as many fish as possible, we began preserving them. We'd have plenty to eat next winter because our crops were growing well at both Tentholm and Falconhurst. Our animals were also thriving. In fact, we had so many animals that we built a farm called Woodlands.
One of our new animals was a bull that had been born during the rainy season.
"Who'll take charge of this fine animal?" I asked my sons.
"I'd rather train Knips," said Ernest as the monkey climbed on his shoulder.
"I'm too busy with my buffalo and jackal," said Jack.
"I don't need another animal," said Fritz, who was in charge of Lightfoot the donkey, and Pounce the eagle.
Meanwhile my wife and I had our own charges. The boys had elected her mistress of Grizzle, the donkey, while I was made supervisor of all the animals. That left Franz as caretaker of the bull.
"I'll call him Grumble," he said happily. "Because of that low grumbling sound he makes."

For two months we worked on completing Rockburg, our new home in the cave. One morning just after we finished, I realized it was the anniversary of our escape from the wreck. Throughout the morning I pondered how we should mark this occasion. At lunch I announced that we would celebrate with a day of thanksgiving and athletic contests.
"Will we run races?" asked Ernest.
"Will there be prizes?" little Franz asked eagerly.
"Yes, there will be prizes," I replied. "Mother and I will be the judges. Now, trumpeters, announce the opening of the games!"
I clapped my hands loudly. Startled, our ducks and geese responded with loud quacks and honks. This amused the boys, who were eager to begin the competition.
"Let's have shooting first," I said.
I set up a target and the boys tried to hit the bull's-eye. After taking turns with a gun, they tried again with bow and arrow. Although Fritz was declared the winner, all my sons were very skilled.
The next event was a race for the three older boys.
"Run to Falconhurst," I said, "and retrieve the jackknife I accidentally left behind. It should be on the table near my bed. The first one back with the knife will be the winner. Ready, set, go!"
Fritz and Jack took off at top speed while Ernest set a slow, steady pace.
"I predict Ernest will win," said my wife.
Long before we expected anyone back, we heard a tremendous galloping sound. Jack rode up on his buffalo with the two donkeys tearing after him. He shouted merrily as he dashed up to us.
"You were supposed to race on your own two feet!" I said.
"I didn't have a chance of winning, so I caught Storm and made him gallop back. Grizzle and Lightfoot decided to join me."
After a while the other boys arrived. Ernest held up the jackknife.
"I got to Falconhurst at least two minutes ahead of Fritz," he said.
"Well done," I said. "And now it's time for climbing."
In this contest Jack performed wonders. He ascended the highest palm trees with remarkable agility. Fritz and Ernest climbed well but couldn't equal the skill of their younger brother.
Riding came next with Jack performing the best. I thought this event was over until little Franz appeared leading Grumble. The young bull was wearing a saddle and bridle.
Franz saluted us. "Prepare to see something new and wonderful!"
Holding the end of a long lead, he gave a series of commands. Grumble proceeded to walk, trot, and gallop. Then Franz mounted the bull and rode awkwardly in a circle.

The final contest was swimming, and Fritz showed himself to be a master of the sport. Meanwhile my wife had returned to Rockburg to prepare the prizes. I found her seated with the prizes laid out by her side. The boys marched in, pretending to play various instruments. They bowed before her as if she were a queen.
"For skill in shooting and swimming . . ." She paused dramatically. "I give this rifle and hunting knife to Fritz."
As the winner of the race to Falconhurst, Ernest received a handsome gold watch. Jack was awarded a pair of silver-plated spurs and a whip for his skill at climbing and riding.
"And now a special prize," said my wife. "For extraordinary skill in bull-training, I present these stirrups to Franz."
We closed the day by remembering everything that had happened a year ago and giving thanks for our new life.

The months passed quickly. Lightfoot, our wild donkey, produced a foal that we named Swift. We built a porch across the front of Rockburg. Aside from those events, all was quiet until Jack had a misadventure one afternoon. He often went off by himself and came back with new things to show us. But this time he reappeared covered with mud and almost in tears.
"What happened?" I said. "Where have you been?"
"I went to get reeds to make baskets, and I fell into the swamp. I called and called for help. But nobody came and I kept sinking."
He had finally managed to cut some reeds and fasten them into a bundle. Meanwhile Fangs, his jackal, had run back and forth at the edge of the swamp.
"I used the reeds like a raft to keep from sinking," said Jack. "When I finally freed my legs from the swamp, I caught hold of Fangs. He pulled me to dry land!"
"Fangs is truly a hero," I said. "But next time take one of your brothers along."
We wanted to make baskets because we needed something for gathering and storing fruits and root vegetables. After some trial and effort, we produced a good supply of baskets.
One basket was especially large. While weaving it, I left holes so that a strong stick could be passed through the holes. In that way two people could carry the basket when it was full and heavy.
"Do you see how this will work?" I asked the boys.
"Oh, yes!" Jack's eyes lit up with fun.
He and Ernest ran a sturdy piece of bamboo through the holes. Then Fritz popped little Franz into the basket. The boys took turns carrying Franz around while he whooped with delight.
"Oh, Father!" cried Fritz. "Don't you think we could make something like this for Mother? It would be more comfortable for her than jolting along in our cart."
The boys shouted with glee at the proposal.
"What do you think, Mother?" asked Ernest.
"Well, I think you could make it, but . . ." She hesitated. "I'm not sure I'd like sitting in the middle of a big basket, peering over the rim."
"We wouldn't make you sit on the bottom of a basket." I laughed. "We'd make you a comfortable seat."
"It would be a bit like a sedan chair," explained Ernest. "I've seen pictures of those in books."
"Yes," I replied, "but who would carry this chair?" I worried that the boys would grow tired or stumble, and then the chair would fall.
"The bull and the buffalo!" cried Jack. "Why not use them? Let's try them now!"
Off ran the boys, and in a short time the basket was securely hung between the two animals. Fritz and Jack sprang into their saddles, and Ernest very carefully deposited himself in the basket.
They set forth at a slow, steady pace. The animals, who were quite docile, appeared only a little surprised at their new task.
"Oh, it's so pleasant, Mother!" called out Ernest as they passed us. "The basket rocks as gently as a cradle. Faster, Fritz, faster!"
Fritz and Jack urged their animals to trot, and Ernest liked that ride too. But then the pace quickened, making the basket shake violently.
"Stop, Fritz!" yelled Ernest. "Halt, Jack! Stop now! Can anybody hear me?"
But Fritz and Jack thought it was great fun to shake up their brother.
"What's the matter, professor?" called Jack. "Didn't sedan chairs go this fast in those books you read?"

The boys made a circuit of the level ground in front of Rockburg. They finally pulled up in front of us like performers awaiting applause. It was hard not to laugh, but Ernest was very angry with them.
"You could have killed me!" he cried angrily.
"Don't be ridiculous," said Fritz. "You're acting like—"
"Quiet, everyone," I said for I could see an argument building up. "Taking a joke too far can only lead to bad feelings. If we're going to survive, we need to keep peace among ourselves."

Fritz and Jack apologized, and Ernest helped them to unharness the bull and buffalo. Then Fritz joined my wife and me on the front porch while the other boys played below. We were chatting pleasantly when Fritz suddenly stood up and stared off into the distance.
"Something strange is coming toward the bridge," he said. "First it was coiled up on the ground like a hose. Now it's rising up and sinking back again."
"Take the other boys inside at once," I told my wife. "Close the door."
Fritz stayed by my side while I examined the object through my telescope.
"It's just as I feared," I said, laying down the telescope. "A giant snake is advancing toward us!"
I joined my family, who were safely inside Rockburg. With pounding hearts, we watched the giant snake's approach.
"It's a boa constrictor!" I whispered.
The boys fired their guns, one right after another. I also fired and missed. Startled but unhurt, the snake glided into the nearby marsh.
"No one is to leave the cave without my permission," I said sternly. "That is a very dangerous snake!"

For three days we—and our animals—stayed inside. The ducks and geese were still out on the marsh. I knew the snake must be lurking in the reeds because the birds were so restless. We were running out of hay for the animals. I was debating what to do when I looked out and saw the snake approaching again. Grabbing my gun, I fired at the snake, and this time I did not miss.
After this episode I decided to take my family to our farm at Woodlands. The boys were soon bored, so I said they could go on an expedition without me. I wanted to encourage their independence.
"I'd rather stay here with you and Mother," said Ernest.
"Not me," said little Franz. "I can't wait to go exploring!"

I would have preferred to keep Franz with us. But I had made the offer to all the boys, so I couldn't withdraw it. In high spirits, the three boys rode off. All day I wondered about their adventures. At sunset they returned and joined us around the campfire.
"We had a splendid ride!" said Jack.
"We went all the way through the Gap!" said little Franz. He was talking about a narrow pass we'd previously found through the rocky hills.
"They're forgetting the most important thing," Fritz said impatiently. "We drove a herd of antelope right through the Gap! The antelope are in our territory now. All ready for us to hunt or tame."
"That's wonderful," I said. "But what's to keep them there, Fritz?"
"We strung a line across the pass—"
"And hung feathers and rags from it," interrupted Franz.
"Those things will dance in the wind and spook the antelope," explained Fritz. "I'm sure the herd won't try to go through the Gap."
"Well done," I said. "Tomorrow I'd like to go out riding with you."
The next day we rode to the Gap. I helped the boys to build a fence of bamboo.
"That ought to keep the antelope on our side of the Gap," I said.

We were on our way back to Woodlands when Jack and Franz decided to gallop ahead. Suddenly four ostriches rose up from where they'd been resting. Jack brought down the large male ostrich with his lasso. We leaped from our steeds and tried to approach the captured bird. He kicked and struggled so hard that I feared we'd have to let him go.
"If only we could block out the light," said Fritz. "Sometimes that calms birds—like putting a cover over a parrot's cage."
I threw my coat over the bird's head, and he stopped struggling.
"How are we going to get him home?" asked Jack.
"I've heard it's possible to tame a wild elephant by making it walk between two tame elephants," I said. "Maybe that would work here."
"But, Father, we don't have any tame ostriches," said little Franz.
"We have Storm and Grumble," Jack pointed out. "I don't think they'll object to helping us."

So we fastened the ostrich between the buffalo and the bull. Franz and Jack mounted their steeds. I removed my coat from the ostrich's head. For a few moments he lay perfectly still. Then he bounded up and tried to escape. But Storm and Grumble weren't about to let him do that.
We slowly walked our prisoner home. As we approached, I could see the look of dismay on my wife's face.
"See what we've got!" crowed little Franz. "An ostrich!"
"Another mouth to feed!" my wife exclaimed. "You've brought home a useless pet!"
"He's not useless, Mother," protested Jack. "You should see how fast he runs. He'll be the fastest animal in our stables. Just wait and see."
A month later the ostrich was completely tame. Jack named him Hurricane.

I made a saddle and a special bridle. The reins were attached to flaps over the bird's eyes. With both flaps open, the bird galloped straight ahead. Cover his right eye and he turned left. Cover his left eye and he turned right. Cover both eyes and he stopped.
Jack took him out for a ride, and the bird galloped away.
"Forget Hurricane," Jack said breathlessly when they returned. "This bird's name should be Hurry."

All the boys were eager to ride Hurry. The ostrich traveled unbelievably quickly from Rockburg to Falconhurst. His speed led the boys to quarrel over who should own him. So I had to step in and end the arguing.
"Hurry belongs to Jack," I said. "Jack weighs less than Fritz or Ernest, so he is more suited to ride the bird. And Franz is not yet strong enough to manage such a fast animal."
Fritz started to protest. "But Father—"
"And," I continued. "Jack was the one who captured him and named him. But you may all practice riding him occasionally. And anyone may ride him in an emergency."
"Thank you, Father," said Jack. "But you must make me some goggles. Sometimes Hurry goes so fast that I have to shut my eyes to protect them from the wind."
"Really?" I said. "I must do no such thing."
"Why not?" Jack looked at me with amazement.
"First because you cannot tell me I 'must' do anything. And second because you are perfectly capable of making goggles yourself."
"I guess I do need an indoor activity," said Jack.

Indeed our outdoor activities were coming to an end. Great black clouds and violent storms marked the beginning of another rainy season. Rockburg was a more spacious and pleasant place to spend the winter than Falconhurst. And we had many activities to keep us busy. Still the time dragged for all of us.
"Let's build a kayak," said Fritz one day. "I've often longed for a more manageable boat than the canoe or the sailboat."
"Oh yes, Father!" pleaded Ernest. "I've read about the kayaks that people build in Greenland."
All the boys were immediately enthusiastic about the idea. But my wife was not.
"'Your chances of drowning are already great enough with the canoe and the sailboat," she declared.
"This is going to be a very safe boat," I reassured her.

We started our boat-building by constructing a frame of whalebone. Then we used bamboo to strengthen the sides and build the deck. That covered the whole length of the boat, leaving only a small square hole to sit in.

We were totally caught up in our work. By the time the kayak was complete, the rainy season was over. The kayak was just narrow enough to fit through our front door. We completed its construction in the open air.
"That's a funny-looking boat," said little Franz. "Do you really think it will float?"
"Look," said Fritz. "It's so light that I can pick it up with one hand."
"It still seems awfully fragile to me," said my wife.
Before she would allow him to try the kayak, she insisted on making him a special swimsuit.
"I don't want him to drown if his boat is punctured by a sharp rock," she explained.
"The kayak won't break like a soap bubble," I said with some exasperation. But I agreed to help her make the swimsuit.
